questions.question: What is a Spring Boot starter dependency?
questions.title: What are Spring Boot starters?
questions.direct_answer: A starter is a curated, pre-tested set of dependencies bundled into a single Maven/Gradle artifact. Instead of manually adding spring-webmvc, jackson-databind, tomcat-embed, and getting the versions right, you add spring-boot-starter-web and get all of those automatically with compatible versions.
questions.interviewer_intent: Basic starter knowledge — test whether the candidate understands what starters do and why they exist.

sections.content: Before starters, to build a Spring web app you'd have to know which individual JARs you needed: spring-webmvc, jackson-databind, javax.servlet-api, tomcat-embed-core, and more. And you'd need to get the versions right so they all work together. A starter collapses all of that into one dependency. spring-boot-starter-web pulls in Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON, and embedded Tomcat — all at versions verified to work together. The naming pattern is spring-boot-starter-{feature}. Web, data-jpa, security, test, mail — one line in your pom.xml per concern.

<dependencies>
  <!-- Pulls in Spring MVC + Jackson + embedded Tomcat -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <!-- Pulls in Hibernate + Spring Data JPA + JDBC -->
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
Starters = one dependency that pulls in a whole feature stack with pre-tested compatible versions.

speakable_v2.hook: Before starters, you had to manually pick a dozen compatible JAR versions for a basic web app. Starters collapse all that into one line.

beats.text: A starter is a single Maven or Gradle dependency that bundles a curated, pre-tested set of libraries for a specific feature. spring-boot-starter-web, for example, pulls in Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON serialization, and embedded Tomcat — all at versions that are verified to work together. You add one line to your pom.xml and the entire web stack is available.

The naming convention is spring-boot-starter-{feature}. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application you'd typically have starter-web, starter-data-jpa, and starter-test as a minimum. No version numbers needed — the parent POM supplies compatible versions for everything the starter pulls in.

questions.question: What are the most commonly used Spring Boot starters?
questions.title: Common Spring Boot starters and what they provide
questions.direct_answer: The most common starters are: spring-boot-starter-web (REST APIs, Spring MVC, embedded Tomcat), spring-boot-starter-data-jpa (Hibernate, Spring Data, JDBC), spring-boot-starter-security (Spring Security), spring-boot-starter-test (JUnit, Mockito, MockMvc), spring-boot-starter-actuator (health/metrics endpoints), spring-boot-starter-validation (Bean Validation).
questions.interviewer_intent: Practical knowledge check — the candidate should know the standard starters from memory.

sections.content: These are the ones you'll use on almost every project. starter-web is for building REST APIs. starter-data-jpa is for database access with JPA and repositories. starter-security adds authentication. starter-test is essential — it brings in JUnit 5, Mockito, and Spring's testing support. starter-actuator adds production monitoring endpoints. starter-validation adds @NotNull, @Size, @Email and the validation framework. For messaging you'd add starter-amqp for RabbitMQ or starter-kafka. For caching, starter-cache. Each one is well-documented at docs.spring.io.

speakable_v2.hook: There are six starters you'll see in almost every Spring Boot project. Knowing what each one provides is table stakes for interviews.

beats.text: These six starters cover the core needs of a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application. Memorize what each one pulls in.

Beyond these six, you'd add starter-amqp for RabbitMQ, starter-kafka for Kafka, or starter-cache for caching. The naming pattern is always spring-boot-starter-{feature}, so it's easy to look up new ones.

questions.question: What does spring-boot-starter-test include, and what is @SpringBootTest?
questions.title: spring-boot-starter-test and @SpringBootTest
questions.direct_answer: spring-boot-starter-test includes JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Hamcrest, MockMvc, and Spring Boot's testing support. @SpringBootTest is an annotation that loads the full ApplicationContext for integration tests, starting the complete Spring context including auto-configuration — unlike unit tests which don't need a context at all.
questions.interviewer_intent: Testing is a core skill — verify the candidate knows the test starter and the difference between unit and integration tests in Spring Boot.

sections.content: The test starter gives you everything you need for both unit and integration tests. JUnit 5 is the test runner. Mockito is for mocking dependencies. AssertJ for fluent assertions. MockMvc for testing HTTP endpoints without starting a real server. @SpringBootTest is for integration tests that need the full Spring context — it's heavier, slower to start, but lets you test the whole stack. For unit tests of a service class, you don't need @SpringBootTest at all — just use Mockito. The distinction matters for test performance.
@SpringBootTest = full context = slower. Unit tests with Mockito = no context = fast. Use both appropriately.

speakable_v2.hook: The test starter gives you a full testing toolkit — and @SpringBootTest is the heavyweight option you use only when you need the full Spring context.

beats.text: spring-boot-starter-test is added automatically by Spring Initializr with test scope. It bundles everything you need for testing a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application.

items: JUnit 5 — the test runner and assertion framework.
Mockito — for mocking dependencies in unit tests.
AssertJ — fluent assertion library for readable test conditions.
MockMvc — tests your HTTP endpoints without starting the real embedded server.
@SpringBootTest — loads the full ApplicationContext for integration tests.

beats.text: The key distinction: @SpringBootTest is slow because it boots the entire Spring context. For unit tests of a service class, skip it — just use Mockito with no Spring context at all. Reserve @SpringBootTest for true integration tests where you need the full stack. Mixing them up leads to a test suite that runs much slower than it needs to.

questions.question: What is the difference between spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-webflux?
questions.title: starter-web vs starter-webflux
questions.direct_answer: spring-boot-starter-web uses Spring MVC, Tomcat, and the traditional blocking servlet model — one thread per request. spring-boot-starter-webflux uses Spring WebFlux, Netty, and the reactive non-blocking model — fewer threads, better for high-concurrency or streaming use cases. They use different programming models and cannot be used together without configuration.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests awareness of the reactive stack — even freshers should know these two models exist.

sections.content: starter-web is the traditional, blocking model. A request comes in, a thread is assigned to handle it, that thread waits while it queries the database, waits while it calls another service. Under high load, all threads get busy waiting. starter-webflux is the reactive model. A request comes in and is handled with callbacks — the thread is freed while waiting for I/O and picks up the result when it's ready. You can handle far more concurrent connections with fewer threads. For most business applications, starter-web is simpler and perfectly adequate. Webflux shines for high-throughput, I/O-heavy, or streaming scenarios.

speakable_v2.hook: starter-web and starter-webflux are two completely different programming stacks — blocking versus non-blocking.

beats.text: The difference goes deeper than just the server — it's a different execution model. Here's the comparison.

For a typical Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, starter-web is the right choice. It's simpler, has better library compatibility, and most business apps don't need the non-blocking benefits. starter-webflux is worth considering when you're building something with high concurrency, streaming responses, or many slow external I/O calls where you want to avoid blocking threads.

questions.question: How do you add a database driver dependency alongside spring-boot-starter-data-jpa?
questions.title: Adding a database driver with spring-boot-starter-data-jpa
questions.direct_answer: spring-boot-starter-data-jpa includes Hibernate and Spring Data JPA but not the specific database driver — that must be added separately. For PostgreSQL add postgresql, for MySQL add mysql-connector-j, for H2 (in-memory) add h2. You must also configure spring.datasource.url, username, and password in application.properties.
questions.interviewer_intent: Very practical — many freshers know about the JPA starter but don't know they also need a driver.

sections.content: A common mistake is adding spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and then wondering why the app fails to start with 'Cannot determine embedded database driver class'. The JPA starter knows how to talk JPA, but it doesn't include a JDBC driver for any specific database. You add that separately. For PostgreSQL, add the postgresql dependency. For MySQL, mysql-connector-j. For testing and local dev, h2 is an in-memory database that's extremely convenient — add it with test scope so it's not in your production JAR.
JPA starter + database driver = both required. Driver scope should be 'runtime' — you don't compile against it directly.

speakable_v2.hook: Adding starter-data-jpa is not enough — you also need a JDBC driver. Miss that and your app won't start.

beats.text: starter-data-jpa includes Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, and the JDBC abstraction layer — but not the actual driver for your specific database. That's a separate dependency. Here's what to add for each common database.

items: H2 (in-memory for tests): com.h2database:h2 with test scope — keeps it out of your production JAR.

beats.text: The scope matters. Runtime scope means the driver is available when the app runs but you don't compile against it — you never import JDBC driver classes directly. Test scope means it's only on the classpath during tests. In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, you'd typically have the real driver in runtime scope and H2 in test scope.

questions.question: What is spring-boot-starter-validation and how is it used?
questions.title: spring-boot-starter-validation and Bean Validation
questions.direct_answer: spring-boot-starter-validation adds Hibernate Validator which implements the Bean Validation API (JSR-380). It lets you annotate fields with @NotNull, @Size, @Email, @Min, @Max, etc. Combined with @Valid on a controller method parameter, Spring automatically validates the incoming request body and returns a 400 if validation fails.
questions.interviewer_intent: Input validation is fundamental for REST APIs — tests whether the candidate knows the Spring Boot validation pattern.

sections.content: Bean Validation lets you put constraints directly on your model class fields. You annotate a field with @NotNull or @Email, and when Spring receives a request it validates the incoming JSON against those annotations before calling your method. If validation fails, it returns a 400 Bad Request automatically. Before this existed, every service method would manually check if (name == null) — repetitive and easy to miss. With Bean Validation you declare what's valid, Spring enforces it. The @Valid annotation on the @RequestBody parameter is the switch that activates validation.
@Valid triggers validation. MethodArgumentNotValidException is thrown on failure — Spring returns 400 by default.

speakable_v2.hook: Instead of writing if (name == null) checks everywhere, you declare constraints on your model and Spring enforces them automatically.

beats.text: starter-validation adds Hibernate Validator — the implementation of the Bean Validation API. You annotate your request DTO fields: @NotBlank, @Email, @Min, @Max, and similar. Then add @Valid to the @RequestBody parameter in your controller. Spring validates the incoming JSON before your method runs. If any constraint fails, it throws MethodArgumentNotValidException and returns a 400 Bad Request automatically.

In a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application, this pattern keeps validation logic out of your service methods. Your service can assume the data is valid because the controller already rejected bad inputs. The two-piece setup is: annotate the DTO, add @Valid to the controller parameter. That's it — no manual if-null checks needed.

questions.question: How do you exclude a transitive dependency from a Spring Boot starter?
questions.title: Excluding transitive dependencies from starters
questions.direct_answer: Use Maven's exclusion mechanism in the dependency declaration. Common use case: exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from spring-boot-starter-web to use Jetty instead, or exclude logback from spring-boot-starter to use Log4j2. Gradle uses the same concept with the exclude() closure.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests practical dependency management knowledge — shows the candidate can work with real-world build configurations.

sections.content: The most common exclusion scenario is swapping the embedded server. starter-web pulls in Tomcat by default. If you prefer Jetty — maybe because it's more lightweight or your team is more familiar with it — you exclude the Tomcat starter from spring-boot-starter-web and add spring-boot-starter-jetty. Another common case is logging: Boot defaults to Logback but some teams use Log4j2. You'd exclude the Logback bridge from the logging starter and add spring-boot-starter-log4j2. The exclusion mechanism is standard Maven — it's not Boot-specific.
Exclude and replace pattern: exclude the default component, add your preferred alternative. Works for servers, logging, connection pools.

speakable_v2.hook: Starters pull in defaults. When you want to swap one out — like Tomcat for Jetty — you use the exclude-and-replace pattern.

beats.text: The pattern is always the same: add the starter with an exclusion block to remove the default, then add the alternative as a separate dependency. Two most common cases in a Spring Boot 3.2 REST API application. First: swapping the embedded server — exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from starter-web, then add spring-boot-starter-jetty or spring-boot-starter-undertow. Second: swapping the logging framework — exclude logback from spring-boot-starter, then add spring-boot-starter-log4j2.

This is standard Maven exclusion syntax — nothing Spring Boot specific. Gradle uses the same idea with the exclude() closure in your dependency declaration. The key thing to understand is why it works: Boot's auto-configuration uses @ConditionalOnClass, so when Tomcat is no longer on the classpath, Tomcat auto-configuration simply doesn't fire. Jetty's auto-configuration fires instead.
